scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Haitian dance originated from a blend of African, European, and indigenous Taíno influences during the colonial period of Saint-Domingue (1501–1804).
Early dances like Méringue emerged from creolisation, combining African rhythms and European ballroom elements.
The Catholic Church opposed African-derived dances, labeling practitioners as black magic.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Dance in Haiti serves religious, social, and political functions.
Vodou dances are sacred rituals connecting practitioners with spirits and ancestors.
Battle dances commemorate revolutionary history and military victories.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage: Divine Horseman The Living Gods Of Haiti - Maya Deren (1947-54) (https://archive.org/details/divine-horseman-the-living-gods-of-haiti-maya-deren-1947-54)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Haitian dance includes diverse styles with varied formations and movements.
Méringue is a partner ballroom dance with a slower tempo and string-based orchestration, featuring graceful, flowing movements.
Kontradans involves four couples performing fast-paced figures without touching, exchanging places in patterns called '8'.
Watch for Yanvalou, Banda pelvic sway, Kontradans figure-eight.
on_screen: Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Couples in ballroom dances; groups in circles or lines for ritual dances; four couples in Kontradans

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Haitian dance music features a mix of African-derived rhythms and European instrumentation.
Méringue uses string instruments like guitar and banjo, saxophone, trap drums, and Congo drums.
Listen for the drums (Rada, Petro, Congo), guitar, banjo, saxophone.
The pulse is Mostly duple (2/4 or 4/4), with polyrhythmic layering in Vodou music at about 90 beats a minute.

A layered soundscape combining steady, syncopated drum rhythms with melodic string and horn instruments; vocals alternate between chant-like spiritual calls and lyrical melodies; mood shifts from calm and fluid in ritual dances to energetic and celebratory in social dances.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Katherine Dunham documented and popularized Haitian dance internationally, integrating it into her choreography and scholarship.
Jean-Léon Destiné founded Haiti's national ballet and taught Haitian dance in the US, promoting African Haitian dance forms.

Vodou dances vary by rite: Rada dances from northern Haiti feature calm, fluid movements; Petro dances from central and southern regions are aggressive and fiery; Gede dances relate to death and fertility, celebrated on All Souls' Day.
Haitian dance descends from African tribal dances (Kongo, Dahomey, Igbo), European ballroom dances (Contra dance, French court dances), and indigenous Taíno traditions.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Haitian dance is parent of Méringue: National dance blending African and European elements.
Haitian dance is child of Kompa: Modern evolution of Méringue with jazz and Cuban influences.
Haitian dance is sibling of Rara: Festival street music and dance with Vodou and Catholic roots.
Haitian dance is sibling of Vodou dance: Sacred ritual dances with polyrhythmic drumming.

visual_brief.costume_notes: Costumes vary by dance style and occasion. Vodou ritual dances feature vibrant, symbolic costumes reflecting spirits and rites, often including masks and specific colors. Battle dances and folk troupes wear attire linked to their historical or social context. Méringue and Kompa dancers typically wear elegant ballroom or social dance clothing. Dance settings range from street festivals like Rara processions to formal theater performances by ballet folklorique companies. Celebrations such as Carnaval des Fleurs and Koudyay festivals provide communal spaces for dance expression.
visual_brief.setting_notes: Dance in Haiti serves religious, social, and political functions. Vodou dances are sacred rituals connecting practitioners with spirits and ancestors. Battle dances commemorate revolutionary history and military victories. Social dances like Méringue and Kompa express cultural identity and community bonding. Festivals such as Rara celebrate slave revolution heritage and religious syncretism. Dance also acts as resistance against oppression and a means of uplifting spirits amid hardship, exemplified by the proverb 'Apre Dans, Tanbou Lou' ('After dance, drums are heavy').
